A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Agentic Predictor. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, formatting, and expanded evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original prediction experiments, component ablations, pretraining analyses, and workflow optimization and transfer results in Section 4 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds workflow populations, backbone comparisons, LLM predictors, resource measurements, and out-of-distribution experiments in Section 4 and Appendix B.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 substantially changes the reported pretraining procedure. v1 selects successful same-task workflows as contrastive positives and failed or mismatched workflows as negatives. v2 instead pairs different views of the same workflow, uses other batch configurations as negatives, and symmetrizes across three modality pairs without performance labels. The main multi-view predictor remains.

E1.justification: v1's predictor benchmark uses only AFlow workflows; v2 adds the independently generated G-Designer workflow population and cross-system and disjoint-domain generalization scenarios (Tables 2–3 and 10–12). The original downstream datasets, including the appendix DROP and HotpotQA transfer evaluations, are retained.

E2.justification: Dir-GNN joins the main comparison, including the retained AFlow settings. Table 9 adds GPT-4.1, Claude 4 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.5 Flash as few-shot LLM performance predictors, substantially expanding comparator types. The original predictive and workflow-optimization comparators remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces cross-framework and six cross-domain train/test protocols, controlled GNN and controller-LLM substitutions, and five-shot LLM classification at temperature zero on up to 1,000 samples per task. It also adds training/inference resource profiling. The original split percentages, supervised training budget, accuracy metric, and utility metric remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to four controller LLMs and five GNN backbones, robustness under framework/domain shifts, and computational efficiency (Section 4.4 and Appendices B.1–B.4). The original input-view, graph-view, label-ratio, transfer, and case-study analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Tables 4 and 5 remove the standard deviations previously reported for the retained ablation means. Three-run averaging and Table 3 uncertainty reporting remain. The seed rule, 2^r, moves from a footnote to the Reproducibility Statement; no increase in runs is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial G-Designer, backbone, LLM, cost, and OOD results; Table 10 newly reports Agentic Predictor averages of 62.05 accuracy and 58.49 utility. Its original AFlow entries remain, while Table 3's average accuracy changes from 84.38 to 79.97 because coverage expands. Retained AFlow utility standard deviations change from 3.18 to 1.18 for GCN and 1.98 to 0.98 for GCN-II. v1 Table 6's optimization results are retained as v2 Table 13.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 redefines the positive and negative sets underlying the contrastive objective and specifies symmetric averaging across three modality pairs, changing its mathematical specification. The general optimization problem and loss templates remain; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The central multi-view prediction and label-efficient pretraining contributions remain. v2 narrows the introduction's 'first predictive framework' claim to an 'underexplored problem' and the abstract's state-of-the-art comparison to several strong graph baselines. Headline improvements change from 12.12%/15.16% to explicitly averaged 6.90%/5.87% under expanded coverage.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of transfer to unseen agents/tools through structural and textual features, backbone robustness including the Mistral exception, and prompted LLM predictors' weaknesses. It qualifies zero search cost by excluding workflow-generation/update costs, adds amortization reasoning, and identifies independently curated benchmarks as a remaining evaluation need.

D1.justification: v2 documents node-aligned graph construction, attention/readout operations, the GCN backbone, embedding dimensions and token limits, and the 232,104-sample pretraining corpus with sampling and exclusion rules. It adds resource requirements and a source-code repository access statement. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's basic hyperparameters and embedding-model names.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LLM-PP, Dir-GNN, Sentence-BERT, and MONAQ, and removes DS-Agent. Section 2 describes FLORA-Bench as a released single-view benchmark and sharpens distinctions concerning representation, pretraining, and efficiency. The broader positioning around workflow prediction and NAS representation learning remains.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites contribution framing, related-work comparisons, and method explanations. Related-work subsections become paragraph headings, Algorithm 1 moves to a dedicated appendix, and the experimental appendices are reorganized. Acknowledgments, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: The paper adopts a different conference layout with changed typography, text width, and display placement. Tables 2–3 expand to distinguish G-Designer and AFlow, and seven new tables present cost, backbone, LLM, and OOD evidence. Existing figures are retained with resizing or relocation; the optimization table moves from Table 6 to Table 13.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the generalization and efficiency evidence beyond v1's AFlow-only predictor benchmark through G-Designer coverage, disjoint-system/domain tests, LLM comparisons, and resource measurements. It also makes the pretraining specification consistent with its label-free claim and clarifies previously unqualified search-cost reporting. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility. Removing ablation standard deviations weakens reporting, but the gains address central weaknesses in methodological clarity and empirical support.
